title: Every winter, snow covers nearly half the land in the Northern Hemisphere
body: Snow cover in the Northern Hemisphere swings hugely through the year, from about **2 million km²** in August to about **45 million km²** in January, nearly half the land surface of the hemisphere. Each winter, as the north tilts away from the Sun, a white cap spreads south across North America, Europe and Asia, then shrinks back in spring. That cap matters well beyond winter sports: snow reflects sunlight, insulates the plants and animals beneath it, and many rivers that start in mountains or the far north get a large part of their water from snowmelt.

slides.question: In which month is snow cover in the Northern Hemisphere usually smallest?
slides.explanation: It bottoms out in August, at about 2 million km², and peaks in January.

slides.heading: More air than water
slides.text: A snowpack's density is typically about 30% that of water, rising to about 50% by late spring as it settles. So a metre of snow holds much less than a metre of water when it melts.

slides.heading: Fact or myth?

items.text: Snow insulates the ground beneath it
Snow cover peaks in midwinter, in January
A metre of snow melts into a metre of water
Snow only matters for weather while it falls

slides.explanation: Snow keeps the cold off plants and animals below it, reflects sunlight and feeds rivers when it melts, and it is mostly air.
